newsitem.title: USA: WALL ST WEEK AHEAD - Stocks surge seen on rate view.
newsitem.headline: WALL ST WEEK AHEAD - Stocks surge seen on rate view.

text.p: Wall Street sailed further into record territory last week and the trend could continue this week as investors shelve interest rate concerns and a wave of new money comes ashore from Europe.

"There could be a flood of foreign money because of political developments in France, Germany and the U.K.," said Thom Brown of Rutherford Brown and Catherwood. He cited recent political developments in those countries that may delay plans for a single European currency.
"It looks like the (European Monetary union) could be delayed for awhile."
While the fate of interest rates hangs in the balance until Federal Reserve policymakers meet in July, consensus is growing that the central bank will hold rates steady.
The Fed did just that last month after raising rates a quarter point in March, the first increase in more than two years, in a bid to ward off inflation.
"I don't think they (will raise rates) this time," said Rutherford's Brown. "If we raise rates, it would make our goods not competitive overseas," he said.

"The market looks like an unstoppable halfback at the Superbowl; it refuses to slow down," said Alan Ackerman, senior vice president at Fahnestock & Co. "There is a growing consensus that by year-end interest rates will be lower as the consumer curtails spending."

Frank Gretz, a technical analyst at Shields & Co, cited the new high in the New York Stock Exchange finance index as evidence of waning fears of Fed tightening. The finance index closed at a record 409 points Friday.
"While everyone's been worried about the Fed, what financial stocks themselves are doing suggests that the market is not expecting higher interest rates or does not care," Gretz said.
Wall Street will likely get some economic cues from the Producer Price Index for May, which is due out on Friday, but analysts are generally not too concerned about the numbers.

"We always look out for the CPI and PPI," said Fahnestock's Ackerman. "The real issue is the strength of the market and the good feeling we've seen on Wall Street and on Main Street. My sense is this a market unlike any market we've ever seen; the move is extraordinary."
He also cited the ability of tech stocks to bounce back. "This market is rallying on the fact that technology may lead the way," he said.

On the European front, analysts say the left's recent victory in French elections has cast uncertainty over the new government's commitment to the EU pact. Britain has said it is highly unlikely to join the pact at the start of 1999. And a dispute between Germany's central bank and Finance Minister Theo Waigel means he attends the talks in a much weakened political state, analysts said.
"The heightened currency instability in Europe makes dollar-denominated instruments look more attractive," said Michael Metz of Oppenheimer & Co.
Shields' Gretz said he sees the broader markets' ability to keep up with the Dow as a signal that stocks still have higher to go.
"You get into trouble when the Dow is up and not the broader markets," he said, adding that Big Board advances have outpaced declines for the past six trading sessions.
Stocks and bonds rallied after the governmment's May U.S. jobs report eased fears of rising interest rates.

The Dow Jones industrial average surged 130.49 to close at 7,435.78, beating the old mark of 7,383.41 set on May 27. The increase was the sixth-largest in point terms and gave the Dow a gain of 104.74 points for the week.
